# Evaluation of a Novel In-house HIV-1 Genotype Drug Resistance Assay using Clinical Samples in China

**Peijie Gao<sup>1*</sup>, Fengting Yu<sup>2,3</sup>, Xiao zhen Yang<sup>1</sup>, Dan Li<sup>1</sup>, Yalun Shi<sup>1</sup>, Yan Wang<sup>2,3</sup> and Fujie Zhang<sup>2,3</sup>**



## Abstract:

**Background:** HIV drug resistance poses a major challenge for anti-retroviral treatment (ART) and the prevention and control of HIV epidemic.

**Objective:** The study aims to establish a novel in-house assay with high efficiency, named AP in-house method, that would be suitable for HIV-1 drug resistance detection in China.

**Methods:** An in-house HIV-1 genotyping method was used to sequence the partial pol gene from 60 clinical plasma samples; the results of our test were compared with a commercial ViroSeq HIV-1 genotyping system.

**Results:** Among sixty samples, 58(96.7%) were successfully amplified by AP in-house method, 5% of them harbored viral load below 1,000 copies/mL. The genotype distribution was 43.1% CRF_07_BC (25/58), 39.7% CRF01_AE (23/58), 6.9% CRF55_01B (4/58), 5.2% subtype B (3/58) and 5.2% CRF08_BC (3/58). Compared with that of the ViroSeq system, the consistent rate of the nucleotide and amino acid sequences obtained by the AP in-house method was 99.5 ± 0.4% and 99.8 ± 0.4%, respectively. A total of 290 HIV-1 drug resistance mutations were identified by two methods, including 126 nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), 145 non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and 19 protease inhibitors (PIs) resistance mutations. Out of them, 94.1% (273/290) were completely concordant between the AP in-house method and the ViroSeq system.

**Conclusion:** Overall, the evaluation of AP in-house method provided comparable results to those of the ViroSeq system on diversified HIV-1 subtypes in China.

**Keywords:** HIV-1, anti-retroviral treatment, genotype, drug resistance mutation, protease inhibitor, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, non-Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.


## 2. MATERIALS AND METHODS

### 2.1. Clinical Specimens

Sixty stored plasma samples were obtained from patients failing ART (2016-2018) in the anti-HIV treatment program of the 13th Five-Year Plan in China. All these samples had been previously tested for HIV-1 drug resistance by the ViroSeq system and were stored at -80°C. The study was also approved by the Institutional Research Ethics Community of Beijing Ditan Hospital, Capital Medical University with reference No.2019(037)-002, and all participants provided written informed consent.

### 2.2. Viral Load Detection

The HIV-1 viral loads in these patients’ plasma were retested with m2000sp Liquid Handler & m 2000 rt Real Time PCR System (Abbott) following the manufacturer’s protocol, which could be used to evaluate amplification sensitivity for AP in-house method [46, 47].

### 2.3. HIV-1 Drug Resistance Genotyping by ViroSeq System

HIV-1 genotyping was performed with ViroSeq HIV-1 Genotyping System (Abbott molecular) [48, 49]. The analysis procedure followed was according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In this system, HIV-1 RNA is extracted manually from 0.5 mL of plasma, followed by reverse transcription with MuLV reverse transcriptase. After the UNG enzyme destroys any species of DNA containing deoxyuridine and a single 40 cycles PCR with AmpliTaq Gold DNA Polymerase, the PCR yields a 1.8 kb DNA product. PCR products are then purified with PCR Cleanup Kit and sequenced by ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer according to product instruction for user issued by the manufacturer. The resulting sequences are assembled and analyzed using ViroSeq Genotyping System Software.

### 2.4. RNA Extraction and Amplification of HIV-1 Partial Pol Gene in AP In-House Method

Viral RNA for AP in-house method was extracted from 200 μL plasma using TGuideS32 automated nucleic acid extraction system (TIANGEN BIOTECH (Beijing) CO., LTD) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The process of RT-PCR of RNA and PCR was simplified into one tube using PrimeScript™ One StepOne RT-PCR kit, Ver.2.0 (TAKARA, Cat. RR055A), following the manufacturer’s protocol. The primers for RT-PCR were BrF-1 (forward), 5’-TCA CTC TTT GGC AAC AGC CC-3’) and BrF-R2 (reverse), 5’-GGA GTC GTT CCC CAT ATT ACT ATG CTT TC-3’(GAAAGCATATGAATACTGGGGAAAGACCTCC)). Reverse transcription was performed at 50°C 40 min with primer BrF-R2, and the amplification started with an initial denaturation at 94°C for 3 min. 50 cycles of PCR were performed with PCR conditions of 94°C for 30 s, 55°C for 30 s, and 72°C for 1 min following an extension to 72°C for 10 min. The amplification products were identified with 1% agarose gel electrophoresis. For the positive products, DNA sequencing was performed on a 3730XL DNA genetic analyzer (Applied Biosystem, CA, USA), according to manufacturer’s instructions.

### 2.5. Drug Resistance Mutation and Phylogenetic Analysis

The obtained sequences were assembled, aligned and edited using BioEdit software. The sequences were then compared with the HIV-1 reference sequence HXB2 (GenBank accession number K03455) to identify mutations. The sequences were analyzed for drug resistance mutations using the Stanford University HIV Drug Resistance Database (HIVdb version 8.9.1, http://hivdb.stanford.edu) for phenotypic resistance interpretation. The HIV-1 subtypes of partial pol sequences were identified by submitting to the REGA HIV-1 Subtyping Tool Version 3.0 and then confirmed using phylogenetic trees, which was conducted by the neighbor-joining method with 1,000 bootstrap replicates in MEGA 5.0 software. The bootstrap values up to 70% were considered significant.

### 2.6. Sequence Analysis

The evaluation of AP in-house method was done by comparing it with ViroSeq system, which was considered as the gold standard. To assess its accuracy, the concordance rate of nucleotide or amino acid sequences generated was analyzed between the ViroSeq system and AP in-house method. Simply, the proportion (%) of partial discordance and discordance in all obtained nucleotide or amino acid sequences for each sample were calculated.

Drug resistance-associated mutations in protease and reverse transcriptase identified by two methods were compared to evaluate the feasibility and effectiveness of AP in-house method. The partial and complete discordance mutations among all identified HIV-1 drug resistance mutations were calculated as above. Then, the distinctions between AP in-house method and ViroSeq system in partial or complete discordance mutations were characterized.

## 3. RESULTS

### 3.1. Confirmation of HIV-1 Infection and Viral Load Measurement

Sixty clinical specimens were collected from HIV-infected patients with antiviral treatment failure. To confirm HIV status of these specimen, their viral load was retested (Table 1). The median viral loads were 73,918 copies/ml (range from 211 to 3,073, 020 copies/ml). HIV-1 subtypes of 59 samples were identified with sequences obtained from the ViroSeq system by Phylogenetic analyses (Table 1). The HIV-1 subtype included 26 CRF07 BC, 23 CRF01 AE, 4 CRF55 01B, 3 subtype B' and 3 CRF08 BC, as shown in Table 1.

### 3.2. Determination of the Sensitivity and Specificity of AP In-house Method

First, we evaluated the sensitivity of AP in-house method with 60 clinical specimens from patients failing ART in China, of which 58 (96.7%) were amplified and sequenced successfully, shown in Table 1. Of the two specimens that failed in amplification, one had a viral load of 6,800 copies/ml and the other one had a viral load of 211 copies/ml. The former could not be amplified with ViroSeq System, even at viral loads above 1,000 RNA copies/ml. The inability to be amplified could likely be attributed to the compromised quality of this specimen. The remaining specimens could be successfully amplified by using the ViroSeq system. Nonetheless, it is worth noting that the AP in-house method was able to amplify 5 of 6 specimens with a viral load below 1,000 copies/ml (Table 1). The amplification sensitivity of AP in-house method reached a viral load of 1000 copies/ml, consistent with the ViroSeq System.

Next, the specificity of AP in-house to amplify different HIV-1 subtypes or CRF was evaluated on 58 clinical specimens. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that the subtype distribution among these obtained sequences was CRF07 BC (25/58), CRF01 AE (23/58), CRF55 01B (4/58), subtype B (3/58) and CRF08 BC (3/58), as shown in (Table 1 and Fig. 1).

### 3.3. Comparison of Nucleotide Sequences and Amino Acid Sequences Obtained from the AP In-house Method with that from the ViroSeq System

A total of 58 samples were amplified and sequenced successfully by both AP in-house method and ViroSeq system. Phylogenetic analysis showed that sequences from each sample obtained by two methods clustered monophyletically together (Fig. 1). The comparison of nucleotide sequences and amino acid sequences obtained by ViroSeq System and AP in-house method showed 99.5 ± 0.4% and 99.5 ± 0.4% (mean ± SD) nucleotide and amino acid identity, respectively. Among 74,635 nucleotides obtained from 58 samples, 394 nucleotide differences were observed between the two methods which were in 80% of the instances caused by the difference in the detection of nucleotide mixtures (315/394). The other discordances (79/394) resulted from the different nucleotides detected. A total of 24,847 amino acids were identified from 58 samples by two methods. The amino acid discordances were observed at 133 positions (18 at drug resistance positions and others at non-drug resistance positions), 110 in amino acids were partial amino acid discordances.

### 3.4. Comparison of Drug Resistant Mutations Identified by AP In-house Method with that by the ViroSeq System

There were a total of 290 HIV-1 drug resistance mutations in protease and reverse transcriptase identified by ViroSeq system and AP in-house method, including 126 nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), 145 non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and 19 protease inhibitors (PIs) resistance mutations, respectively (Table 2). Among them, partial discordance mutations were observed at 16 positions, and one complete discordance mutation was observed in RT region (Table 3). Out of 16 partial discordance mutations, mixture bases in 12 positions were only identified by the ViroSeq system, and three cases by AP in-house method. The other one at position 101 in RT region was identified with different mixture bases by two methods. Moreover, there was one NNRTI resistance mutation (V179D) that was only observed by AP in-house method but not by the ViroSeq system.
---

### 3.5. Comparison of the Testing Period between AP In-house Method and ViroSeq System

Automation nucleic acid extraction machine was used in our AP in-house method, substituting manual sample preparation in the ViroSeq system, which significantly reduced working time. As shown in Table 4, testing for 32 samples took only 4.5 h for AP in-house method to obtain the PCR products, while ViroSeq system took 10h.



## 4. DISCUSSION

In this study, a cost-effective HIV drug resistance mutation method was designed and optimized as AP in-house method. Compared with other reported in-house methods [50], the extraction of nucleic acid in AP in-house method was improved with instruments rejecting the approach chosen by hand. Moreover, two-step PCR was simplified into one-step, reducing the possibility of cross-contamination and increasing the detection efficiency. It was shown that 32 samples could be extracted and amplified within 4.5 hours by AP in-house method; however, it took 8 hours for the extraction and amplification of 12 samples by commercial kit and 7 hours for 24 samples by the traditional in-house method.

It was reported that HIV-1 circulating subtype B in China was identified, including CRF01 AE, subtype B, CRF07 BC, and CRF08 BC, (43, 51-58) as well as the novel HIV-1 CFRs 58, 59-64 (CRF55 01B [65], CRF59 01B [66], etc). So, the ability to detect mutations on diversified HIV-1 subtypes is necessary for HIV-1 drug resistance assays. Of the 58 samples detected by both methods, there were circulating subtypes in China, which suggested that the specificity of AP in-house method was similar to that of ViroSeq system and AP in-house method could be used for the testing of drug-resistant strains in China. And also, the lowest limit of amplification sensitivity of AP in-house method reached at the viral load of 225 copies/ml, higher than the 1000 copies/ml established by the ViroSeq system and traditional in-house method. All these indicated that this AP in-house method could be applied to HIV-1 drug resistance detection in China.

There is an advantage in the ViroSeq system [50], in which software is designed specifically for the analysis of drug resistance to PIs and RTIs. While for AP in-house method, the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database (HIVDB) was used to analyze drug resistance mutations. Although some of the nucleotide sequences obtained by the two methods were the same, the identified mutations might be a bit different depending on the particular database. For instance, H221Y [67], V106I [68] and K70T [69] were only known as drug resistance mutations in HIVDB; however, L10I, K43T, A71T, A71V, T69N, K101Q and K103R were only identified in ViroSeq system v2.8. Therefore, multiple and updating databases should be used for the most comprehensive testing.

Different from the entire PR designed in the ViroSeq system, the AP in-house method was designed to detect drug re- sistance mutations (DRM) in part of PR (codons 4 to 99) according to HIV-1 subtype B in plasma samples. However, the major and minor drug resistance mutations in PR could be successfully detected by using this AP in-house method because the first common polymorphic/ non-polymorphic ac- cessory PI-selected mutation was first present at position tenth in PR in the Stanford University HIV drug resistance database. Moreover, more than 51 amino acids (codons 336 to 386) in the first part of the RT gene were sequenced using AP in-house method compared to that obtained by using Vi- roSeq system, which could be used to detect more drug-resistant mutations in RT region. N348I [70-75], the additional miscellaneous mutation in the connection domain of the HIV-1 RT region, was detected in two plasma samples (A009 and A024) by using our AP in-house method in this study. Given the Stanford University HIV drug resistance database, N348I could reduce NRTIs Zidovudine susceptibility about 3-fold and NNRTIs Nevirapine and Efavirenz susceptibility by 3-fold and 2-fold, respectively [76]. Furthermore, N348I could enhance the resistance to Etravirine and Rilpivirine [70]. As a result, more positions of drug resistance mutations could be detected by AP in-house method than that in the ViroSeq system, which made it more exten- sive applications in HIV-1 drug resistance detection.

## CONCLUSION

We designed and evaluated an efficient in-house method for the identification of HIV-1 drug resistance mutations. The sensitivity and specificity of AP in-house method were comparable to the ViroSeq system and other assays pub- lished previously [50]. In addition, AP in-house method had the advantage of identifying novel drug resistance mutations located beyond the detectable regions of the ViroSeq sys- tem. The validated AP in-house method could serve as a powerful tool to effectively test patients failing ART and monitor the emergence and transmission of HIV-1 drug resis- tance in China.

#  HIV-1 Group O Resistance Against Integrase Inhibitors

## Abstract

## Background:

HIV-1 group O (HIV-O) is a rare variant that is characterized by a high
number of natural polymorphisms in the integrase coding region that may
impact on susceptibility to integrase strand transfer inhibitors
(INSTIs) and on the emergence of resistance substitutions. We previously
reported that HIV-O is more susceptible to RAL than HIV-1 group M
(HIV-M).

## Methods:

The aim of this study was to assess pathways of resistance to INSTIs in
group 0 variants. Accordingly, we selected for resistance to each of
raltegravir (RAL), elvitegravir (EVG), and dolutegravir (DTG) in cord
blood mononuclear cells using HIV group O subtypes A and B, an HIV-O
divergent isolate, and HIV-1 group M (subtype B, which served as a
reference). Site-directed mutagenesis was performed on the pCOM2.5 HIV
group 0 infectious clone to ascertain the impact of INSTI resistance
substitutions at positions Q148R, N155H, and R263K within integrase on
susceptibility to INSTIs and infectiousness.


## Results:

Cell culture selections of group O variants yielded similar patterns of
resistance to RAL, EVG, and DTG as observed for subtype B. In the DTG
selections, subtype B yielded S153Y, whereas a natural S153A
polymorphism sometimes led to A153V in group O. The pCMO2.5/Q148R and
pCMO2.5/N155H variants displayed far higher levels of resistance to DTG
(\>1000 FC) than was seen for group M viruses.


## Conclusions:

HIV-O harboring Q148R and N155H shows higher resistance to DTG compared
with HIV-M subtype B.


## METHODS


## Viruses and Plasmids

Three viral isolates from HIV-O--infected ARV-naive patients,
representative of each subtype, and 1 from HIV-M subtype B were studied:
11,367 (HIV-O, subtype A, termed HIV-O/A), MVP5180 (HIV-O, subtype B,
termed HIV-O/B), BCF11 (HIV-O, divergent strain, termed HIV-O/Div), and
5326 (HIV-M, subtype B, termed HIV-M). The 11,367 and 5326 viruses were
isolated at the McGill AIDS Center, whereas MVP5180 and BCF11 were
obtained from the NIH AIDS Research and Reference Reagent Program
(catalog numbers 2878 and 4142, respectively).

For in vitro analysis in TZMBl cells, plasmid pNL4-3 (NIH, catalog
number 114) was used as an HIV-M (subtype B) reference virus. The
infectious HIV-O clone pCOM2.5 was graciously provided by HG Kräusslich
(Abteilung, Virologie, Universitätsklinikum Heidelberg, Germany).

26


##   Sequencing and Interpretation of Resistance Genotyping

The integrase region of HIV-O viruses was amplified and sequenced as
previously described.

17

Sequencing results were analyzed using SeqScape software version 2.5.
DNA sequences were compared with those of the HIV-1 group M reference
strain HXB2 using Bioedit software for alignment (BioEdit Sequence
Alignment Editor v7.1.3, Copyright 1997--2011, Tom Hall, Carlsbad, CA).
Major and accessory integrase mutations were defined according to the
latest updated version (March 2, 2014) of the Stanford University HIV
Database ( http://hivdb.stanford.edu/DR/INIResiNote.html ).


##   Site-Directed Mutagenesis in pCMO 2.5 and Production of Viruses

We constructed HIV-O integrase mutants using the infectious clone
pCMO2.5.

26

Four mutants were generated: pCMO2.5/Q148R, pCMO2.5/N155H,
pCMO2.5/R263K, and pCMO2.5/A153S.

The mutagenesis reaction was run for 3 minutes at 98°C, followed by 35
cycles at 98°C for 10 seconds, 57°C for 20 seconds, and 72°C for 10
minutes and a final step at 72°C for 6 minutes using Phusion high
fidelity DNA polymerase (New England BioLabs Inc). Primers for
site-directed mutagenesis were designed using Quikchange primer design
software (Agilent Web site,
http://www.genomics.agilent.com/primerDesignProgram ) ( Table 1 ). Each
plasmid was amplified in **Escherichia coli** XL10-Gold ultracompetent
cells, Tet **r** Δ ( **mcrA** ) 183 Δ **(mcrCB-hsdSMR-mrr)173 endA1
supE44 thi-1 recA1 gyrA96 relA1 lac** Hte \[F′ **proAB lacI** ****q****
**Z** Δ **M15 Tn10** (Tet **r** ) Amy Cam **r** \] (Stratagene, Agilent
Technologies, Mississauga, ON, Canada). Successful mutagenesis was
confirmed by sequencing (Genome Québec).

Each plasmid was transfected into 293T cells (American Type Culture
Collection, CRL-11268) to produce replication-competent wild-type or
mutant virus. Infectiousness and phenotyping experiments were performed
using TZMbl cells (NIH AIDS Research Reagent Program).


##   Resistance Selection in Cord Blood Mononuclear Cells

Selections for drug resistance were performed in cord blood monuclear
cells (CBMCs) as previously described with the following viruses, that is, 11,367 (HIV-O/A), MVP5180
(HIV-O/B), BCF11 (HIV-O/Div), and 5326 (HIV-M), in increasing
concentrations of RAL, EVG, and DTG. Wells for each virus without drug
pressure were included as negative controls. RT activity was monitored
weekly in culture fluids and the latter were also collected weekly for
viral sequencing. The drugs DTG, RAL, and EVG were kindly provided by
GlaxoSmithKline/ViiV Healthcare, Research Triangle Park, NC, Merck Inc,
West Point, PA and Gilead Sciences, Foster City, CA, respectively.


##   Infectiousness in TZMBl Cells

To assess the infectiousness of the different pCMOwt and viral variants,
in comparison with pNL43, we performed infectivity assays using TZMBl
cells (Fig. 1). The results show that all pCMO mutants had levels of
infectivity similar to wt, with the exception of pCMO/A153S, which was
about 3 times more infectious. The pCMOwt and variant viruses were less
infectious than pNL43. These differences are statistically significant (
**P** \< 0.0000001; see the Table within Fig. 1).


##   Susceptibility to INSTIs in TZMbl Cells

To determine the susceptibility of pCMOwt and viral variants to different INSTIs in culture, we used a cell culture--based phenotypic assay with TZMBl cells as previously described.
The EC50 , obtained from 3 independent experiments in triplicate, was calculated using GraphPad Prism software. The results were also expressed on the basis of FC, that is, the ratio of EC50 of a mutated virus EC50 wt, using pCMOwt as a reference (FC = 1).


##   Statistical Analysis

Results were expressed as mean ± standard error with a 95% interval of
confidence. To determine whether differences between HIV-O and HIV-M
viruses were significant, we performed both χ **2** and Student **t**
tests, with **P** \< 0.05 defining a significant difference.


##   RESULTS


##   Tissue Culture Selection of INSTI-Resistant Variants of HIV-O

The selection of INSTI-resistant viruses in CBMCs was performed for 53
weeks and the results are summarized in Table 2 . We were able to reach
higher levels of drug concentrations for HIV-M in comparison with the 3
HIV-O viruses that were tested. In all cases, DTG concentrations could
not be increased as quickly as with RAL and EVG.

The substitutions selected in HIV-O can be classified as follows: (1)
substitutions previously described for HIV-M such as T97A, Q148R,
V151A/I (RAL), T66I, E92Q, E157Q (EVG), and M50I, R263K (DTG) and (2)
substitutions for HIV-O that were not previously described in HIV-M,
that is F121C in HIV-O/B with RAL, V75I in HIV-O/A with RAL, and S153V
in HIV-O/A with DTG. Only the HIV-O/Div variant selected the Q148R
mutation for RAL and R263K plus M50I for DTG, as previously described
for HIV-M.


None of the HIV-O viruses selected either N155H or Y143C that are
associated with resistance to RAL in HIV-M.

Aside from the changes reported in Table 2 , the number of polymorphisms
in the integrase region did not change as a result of DTG pressure,
similar to results with RAL and EVG.


##   Susceptibility of pCMOwt and Mutated Viruses to INSTIs in Tissue Culture

Using TZMBl cells, we showed that pCMO2.5 wt was susceptible to all 3
INSTIs tested and EC50 values and FCs are summarized in the Table
within Figure 2. All pCMO mutated variants were more resistant to RAL
than was pCMO2.5 wt with the exception of pCMO2.5/R263K that displayed a
lower FC (FC = 0.6).

For EVG, the EC50 values for pCMO2.5 mutants were higher than those
of the wt virus (FC 5.6--15) (Table in Fig. 3). Although a high degree
of variability was observed, this is common for this drug.

In the case of DTG (Fig. 4), both pCMO 2.5/Q148R and pCMO 2.5/N155H
possessed high-level resistance (FC \> 1000), whereas pCMO/R263K yielded
approximately the same EC50 value as wt (FC = 1.1). The pCMO/A153S
variant was more susceptible to DTG than wt (FC = 0.08). Statistically
significant differences were observed for all the mutated variants
tested for all INSTIs tested with the exception of pCMO 2.5/R263K and
pCMO 2.5/A153S for DTG (Table in Fig. 4).


##   DISCUSSION

This work presents an analysis of INSTI selective pressure leading to
the emergence of resistance substitutions in representative wt HIV-O
viruses (ie, subtypes A and B, and a divergent strain). Notable
differences were observed for HIV-O in comparison with HIV-M. First, we
attained higher concentrations of each drug at the end of the selections
with HIV-M than with the 3 HIV-O viruses ( Table 2 ), despite the fact
that all viruses were normalized for levels of RT activity. The
emergence of resistant variants occurred as early as week 21 for HIV-M
or HIV-O (data not shown). HIV-O selected the Q148R substitution in the
presence of RAL and T66I or E92Q in the presence of EVG ( Table 2 ).
However, none of the HIV-O viruses selected either N155H or Y143C after
more than 40 weeks of RAL pressure, although both substitutions were
selected in HIV-M. We used only 3 HIV-O variants in our study;
therefore, we cannot be certain that the aforesaid substitutions would
never be selected under RAL pressure in HIV-O, especially since group O
and M viruses bear the same or similar codons at these positions (ie,
AAT in both groups for 155 and TAT or TAC for 148). The accessory
substitution, T97A, was selected by 2 of the 3 HIV-O viruses under RAL
pressure (O/A and O/Div), in association with V151A and Q148R plusV151I,
respectively. Interestingly, HIV-2, which is closely related to HIV-O,
can also select T97A alone without the other major RAL resistant
mutations.

28

It has also been reported that Y143C in HIV-2 integrase had no
statistically significant effect on sensitivity to RAL.

29

To our knowledge, the combination of Q148R plus T97A without G140S has
never previously been reported in HIV-M.

Under DTG pressure, the divergent HIV-O strain selected R263K in
association with M50I, as previously described for HIV-M, in which case
the presence of M50I slightly increased DTG resistance but did not
restore viral replicative fitness.

24,27

HIV-M selected S153Yand HIV-O/A harboring S153A and G163Q natural
polymorphisms selected A153V plus Q163R with R262K ( Table 2 ). S153Y
had previously been selected by DTG and was shown to confer low-level
resistance to each of the 3 INSTIs in HIV-M.

15

The R262K substitution was also selected in culture by DTG in a
pNL43/H51Y variant.

30

Now, we observed that DTG pressure on HIV-O/A first selected a H51H/Y
and R262R/K mixture (week 30; data not shown) and that H51H/Y was
subsequently replaced by A153V (week 42, Table 2 ). This is consistent
with the finding that R262K, in combination with H51Y, slightly
decreased susceptibility to DTG in HIV-M.

31

As illustrated in Table 2 , HIV-0 viral isolates selected for RAL and
EVG resistance more readily than for resistance against DTG. It has
already been reported that HAART could impact on genetic evolution
within integrase.

32--34

In contrast to patients receiving therapy with RAL, treatment with DTG
may disfavor subsequent genetic change due to reduced viral replication
capacity, possibly due to selection of the R263K resistance mutation.

35

The A153V substitution that is selected by DTG in HIV-O is interesting
since the baseline residue at this position is an alanine (A) in HIV-O
instead of serine (S) as in HIV-M. In HIV-M, the relevant resistance
substitution is S153Y (or S153F).

15

A change from A to V (153A **G **C** C** → 153V **G **T** C** ) is
easier than a change from A to tyrosine (Y) (153A **G **C** C** → 153Y
****TA** C** ), since the former requires only a single transition. This
is further evidence of the impact of baseline polymorphisms on the
emergence of drug resistance.

36

We further studied position 153 by mutating the A in HIV-O to S. This
single change in pCMO2.5 increased infectiousness by 70%, close to the
level of HIV-M (pNL43) and statistically different from pCMOwt (FC = 0.3
and 0.13 for pCMO 2.5/A153S and pNL43, respectively; **P** \< 0.0000001;
Fig. 1). Molecular modeling has shown that position 153 is close to the
catalytic site of integrase and plays a role in enzymatic function,

17

consistent with the impairment of integrase activity in HIV-O and
highlighting the importance of the A/S153 residue. Position 153 is also
part of the "minimal integrase region" (residues 53--153) needed for
interaction with the cellular cofactor INI1 (integrase interactor 1)
that is involved in integration of viral DNA.

37

All pCMO variants showed resistance in comparison with wt, with FC
values from 3 to \>1000, except for pCMO/R263K (RAL, DTG) and pCMO/A153S
(DTG). Interestingly, pCMO/A153S displayed a statistically significant
higher change in EC **50** for RAL (FC = 3; **P** \< 0.01), consistent
with observations that HIV-O is more susceptible to RAL than HIV-M, both
in biochemical assays and in tissue culture,

17

perhaps because the 153 residue impacts on INSTI susceptibility in
HIV-O.

In addition, 2 substitutions associated with RAL, that is, Q148R and
N155H, displayed very high-level resistance to DTG, although DTG did not
select for either of these substitutions in culture, making clear that a
high level of resistance to DTG imparted by a single amino-acid change
in group O. In contrast, Q148R and N155H in HIV-M conferred only 1.2-
and 0.99-fold resistance to DTG, respectively,

15

similar to results obtained with simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV).

38

It is interesting to note that HIV group O and HIV-2 seem to share a DTG
resistance profile that is distinct from group M viruses and that a
combination of T97A and Y143C substitutions in HIV-2 yielded \>5000-fold
resistance to DTG.

39

These findings and our own suggest that DTG may be limited if used as
part of a second-line regimen to treat individuals who have first failed
either RAL or EVG, since the drug-resistant mutations associated with
the latter drugs confer cross-resistance to DTG. In contrast, the use of
DTG to treat HIV-2 or group O--infected patients in first-line therapy
would not seem to be contraindicated on the basis of the drug resistance
profile of the latter drug. In fact, the propensity of HIV-1 and HIV-2
of all groups and subtypes, studied to date, to preferentially select
for a R263K resistance-associated mutational pathway that greatly
diminishes viral replicative fitness provides reassurance that DTG may
be safely used in the clinic without exaggerated fear for the
development of drug resistance.


##   CONCLUSIONS

We have shown the selection of INSTI-resistant variants in HIV-O and
have demonstrated the impact of the Q148R, N155H, R263K, and A153S
substitutions in HIV-O on viral infectiousness and susceptibility to
INSTIs.

We have reaffirmed the importance of position 153 in integrase on viral

# Phylogenetic analysis of HIV-1 subtypes and drug resistance profile among treatment-naïve people in Kuwait


## Abstract

Mutations associated with resistance to antiretroviral therapy are a
major cause of failure to treatment, and surveillance for the emergence
of HIV resistance became a component of all antiretroviral treatment
programs. As transmission of resistant viruses to newly infected persons
is possible, we aimed to determine the prevalence of primary mutations
associated with antiretroviral resistance among treatment-naïve
patients, with respect to HIV subtype. Viral RNA was extracted from
plasma samples of 43 treatment-naïve patients. Protease (PR) and reverse
transcriptase (RT) regions were amplified and sequenced using the
TRUGENE HIV-1 Genotyping Assay. A phylogenetic analysis was performed
for HIV subtype assignment. Complete sequence information could be
obtained for 35 patients. A total of ten different HIV-1 subtypes and
recombinant forms were found in Kuwait with predominance of subtypes B,
C, and CRF01_AE. A62V and A98G were non-polymorphic
resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) detected in the RT region of two
and three patients, respectively. Non-polymorphic mutations associated
with resistance to protease inhibitors were not detected. Our results
support continuous surveillance of RAMs in newly infected individuals to
assess the effectiveness of first-line antiretroviral regimen available
in Kuwait. ***J. Med. Virol. 87:1521--1526, 2015* .** © 2015 Wiley
Periodicals, Inc.



## METHODOLOGY

### Study Population

Fourty-three plasma samples were collected from treatment-naïve
HIV-infected patients, between June 2011 and October 2014. Data recorded
for patients included the following variables: file number, birth date,
gender, nationality, and date of diagnosis. The ethical permission on
this research study was granted by the Ethical Decision Committee of the
Research Administration, Faculty of Medicine, Kuwait University, and by
the Standing Committee for Coordination of Health and Medical Research,
Ministry of Health.

### HIV RNA Concentrations

HIV-1 RNA concentrations in the plasma samples of recently diagnosed
HIV-1 patients were determined by real-time PCR using the COBAS
AmpliPrep/COBAS TaqMan HIV-1 test v2.0 (Roche Diagnostic Systems,
Branchburg, NJ) according to the manufacturer\'s instructions.

### HIV-1 Subtype Classification

The isolation of viral RNA from clinical samples was performed using the
automated MagNa Pure LC 2.0 system (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim,
Germany). Amplification and sequencing of 918-bp of *pol* gene were
performed using the TRUGENE HIV-1 Genotyping Assay, on the OpenGene ^®^
automated DNA Sequencing System (Siemens Healthcare Diagnostics,
Norwood, MA). The obtained nucleotide sequences consisting of 980 bp of
the *pol* gene were searched against the NCBI GenBank database using
Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST), and then aligned with all the
HIV reference sequences available in the HIV sequence database (
http://www.hiv.lanl.gov/ ), using ClustalW method in the Molecular
Evolutionary Genetics Analysis (MEGA) software version 4.02 \[Tamura et
al., 2007 \]. Phylogenetic trees were reconstructed using
neighbor-joining method, with evolutionary distances computed using the
Kimura two-parameter method. A bootstrap test with 1,000 replicates was
used to estimate the confidence of branching patterns in the trees. The
accession number of each HIV reference sequence was added to the taxon
label in the phylogenetic tree. The HIV-1 sequence from group O (GenBank
accession number, AY618998) was used as an outgroup. HIV-1 sequences
resulted from this study were uploaded to GenBank (accession numbers
HF937222 to HF937249, KM588925 to KM588956). The recombination form was
further analyzed by performing bootscanning analysis with a sliding
window of 200 bp, incremental steps of 20 bases, and the Kimura
two-parameter model using Simplot 3.5.1 software (Johns Hopkins
University, Baltimore, MD).

### Drug Resistance Assessment

HIV-1 drug resistance was determined by sequencing the reverse
transcriptase and protease regions on the HIV-1 *pol* gene, using the
TRUGENE HIV-1 Genotyping Assay, according to Siemens GuideLines™ Rules
17 (Siemens Healthcare Diagnostics, Norwood, MA). Prevalence of
transmitted drug resistance was estimated using the World Health
Organization (WHO) surveillance drug-resistance mutations list \[Bennett
et al., 2009 \] and Stanford University genotypic resistance
interpretation algorithm ( http://hivdb.stanford.edu/ ).

::: section

## RESULTS

### Patient Baseline Characteristics

The baseline characteristics of treatment-naïve patients with HIV-1
infection are given in Table I . From June 2011 till October 2014, 43
patients (nine females and 34 males) were newly diagnosed positive for
HIV-1. Their age ranged from 2 days to 73 years, with a median age of 33
years. Most of them were Kuwaiti. The median of viral load at sampling
was 7.3 × 10 ^4^ RNA copies/ml (range: undetected to 6.6 × 10 ^5^
copies/ml).


### Subtype Distribution

HIV-1 *Pol* gene sequencing was performed for all HIV-positive samples;
however, complete sequence information was obtained for only 35
patients. According to the phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 1 and Table II ),
subtypes B, C, and CRF01_AE were the most prevalent subtypes. Four HIV-1
isolates clustered together with recombinant forms involving subtypes
CRF01_AE and B: one HIV-1 isolate (05717) clustered with CRF55_01B, with
bootstrap value more than 90%, and three other isolates (06295, 09820,
and 0972) formed two separate clusters with the recombinant forms
CRF15_01B and CRF53_01B, but with bootstrap values of less than 70%.
Other HIV-1 subtypes detected included subtypes A, CRF02_AG, CRF35_AD,
and CRF50_A1D (Table II ). The recombination event in nine of HIV-1
isolates was confirmed by bootscanning analysis (Fig. 2 ). The typing
results of recombination analysis were equivalent to those inferred from
the phylogenetic analysis. In addition, recombination events between
more than two subtypes/CRFs were observed in three isolates (09820,
05717, and 021780).

### Drug Resistance Profile

A62V was the only non-polymorphic NRTI resistance-associated mutation
(RAM) detected in two patients (5.7%) with HIV-1 subtype A infection.
Alone, A62V mutation does not reduce NRTI susceptibility. Three patients
(8.6%) with HIV-1 subtype CRF01_AE infection had the non-polymorphic
A98G RAM that can be associated with reduced NNRTI susceptibility.
Non-polymorphic RAMs in the PR region were not detected in this study.


## DISCUSSION

Kuwait has low-prevalence of HIV-1 infection. Since 1984, when the first
Kuwaiti HIV case was reported, till the end of 2013, a cumulative total
of 252 Kuwaiti HIV cases has been reported, 72.6% male and 27.4% female.
In the period 2012--2013, 46 new Kuwaiti HIV cases were reported
\[UNAIDS, 2014 \]. This explains the low number of patients recruited in
this study.

A total of 10 different subtypes and recombinant forms were detected in
only 28 Kuwaiti patients, suggesting the heterogeneity of HIV epidemic
in Kuwait. Subtypes B, C, and CRF01_AE were the most prevalent subtypes
detected in Kuwait. CRF01_AE subtype dominates in Southeast Asia, mainly
in Thailand where this was first identified in the late 1980s. It has a
global prevalence of ∼5% \[McCutchan, 2000 ; Taylor et al., 2008 \].
Subtype B is found in Americas, western Europe, east Asia, and Oceania
with global prevalence of ∼10%, whereas subtype C is predominant in
India and in eastern and southern Africa with global prevalence of ∼50%
\[Taylor et al., 2008 \]. HIV-1 recombinant forms involving CRF01_AE and
B subtypes were observed in four patients (11%); these CRFs had been
reported in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, and China, mainly among
injecting drug users (IDUs) and men who have sex with men (MSM)
\[Tovanabutra et al., 2007 ; Li et al., 2010 ; Ng et al., 2011 ; Han et
al., 2013 \]. In three patients (8.6%), HIV-1 recombinant forms
involving A and D subtypes were identified. CRF35_AD subtype is
circulating mainly in Iran and Afghanistan, while CRF50_A1D in the
United Kingdom \[Sanders-Buell et al., 2007 ; Jahanbakhsh et al., 2013 ;
Foster et al., 2014 \]. Subtypes A and CRF02_AG were also detected in
this study. Subtype A is prevalent in east and central Africa, central
Asia, eastern Europe with global prevalence of ∼12%, whereas CRF02_AG
subtype is prevalent in west Africa with global prevalence of ∼5%
\[Taylor et al., 2008 \].

Only three patients (8.6%) had HIV-1 sequence mutation (A98G) that may
be associated with reduced susceptibility to NNRTI. A98G ia a
non-polymorphic accessory mutation that reduces nevirapine (NVP)
susceptibility by ∼fivefold and efavirenz (EFV) susceptibility by
∼threefold \[The Stanford HIV Drug Resistance Database, 2014 \]. In
combination with mutations at positions 90, 98, 100, 106, 181, 190,
A98G, mutation causes resistance to etravirine \[Hirsch et al., 2008 ;
Johnson et al., 2013 \]. A62V mutation was detected in two patients with
HIV-1 subtype A, and alone has no effect, but in combination with
mutations at positions 65, 75, 77, 116, 151, causes multi NRTI
resistance \[Shafer et al., 2001 ; The Stanford HIV Drug Resistance
Database, 2014 \]. A62V mutation has been also reported in 16% of
subtype A viruses in former Soviet Union countries but is otherwise
non-polymorphic \[Bennett et al., 2009 \]. Transmission of RAMs and
their effect on the response to first-line ART has been well reported
previously \[Little et al., 2002 ; Gallant et al., 2006 \]. In Kuwait,
the first-line therapeutic regimen is a NNRTI-based regimen (efavirenz
or nevirapine with a combination of two NRTIs, lamivudine or
emtricitabine + tenofovir or abacavir). PI-based regimen is also
available and consists mainly of atazanavir/ritonavir or
darunavir/ritonavir + two NRTIs. When NNRTI- and PI-based regimens fail,
an INSTI (integrase strand transfer inhibitor)-based regimen consisting
of raltegravir + two NRTIs is offered. Patients who harbor mutations
conferring resistance to NNRTI-based regimen will, therefore, benefit
from alternative regimens.

In conclusion, different HIV-1 subtypes are present in Kuwait with
predominance of B, C, and CRF01_AE subtypes. Only three out of 35
treatment-naïve patients with HIV-1 infection had a single mutation that
might be associated with low-level resistance to current NNRTI. These
results highlight the necessity of continuous surveillance of drug
resistance in recently diagnosed patients, thereby reducing the
likelihood of initial treatment regimen failure.

# High prevalence of pre-treatment HIV drug resistance in Papua New Guinea: findings from the first nationally representative pre-treatment HIV drug resistance study
Janet Gare1*, Ben Toto1, Percy Pokeya2, Linh‐Vi Le3, Nick Dala4, Namarola Lote5, Bangan John5, Abel Yamba2, Kevin Soli2, Joshua DeVos6, Heather Paulin7, Nick Wagar6, Du‐Ping Zheng6, Takeshi Nishijima8, Peniel Boas9, Angela Kelly‐Hanku1,10† and Anup Gurung5†

## Abstract

Background: Determining the prevalence of pre‑treatment HIV drug resistance (PDR) is important to assess the effectiveness of first‑line therapies. To determine PDR prevalence in Papua New Guinea (PNG), we conducted a nationally representative survey.

Methods: We used a two‑stage cluster sampling method to recruit HIV treatment initiators with and without prior exposure to antiretroviral therapies (ART) in selected clinics. Dried blood spots were collected and tested for PDR.

Results: A total of 315 sequences were available for analysis. The overall PDR prevalence rate was 18.4% (95% CI 13.8–24.3%). The prevalence of PDR to non‑nucleoside analog reverse‑transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) was 17.8% (95% CI 13.6–23.0%) and of PDR to nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) was 6.3% (95% CI 1.6–17.1%). The PDR prevalence rate among people reinitiating ART was 42.4% (95% CI 29.1–56.4%).

Conclusions: PNG has a high PDR prevalence rate, especially to NNRTI‑based first‑line therapies. Our findings suggest that removing NNRTIs as part of first‑line treatment is warranted and will lead to improving viral suppression rates in PNG.

Keywords: Human immunodeficiency virus, Pre‑treatment drug resistance, Antiretroviral therapy, Papua New Guinea


## Methods

Study design

A cross-sectional survey using a two-stage cluster sampling design based on the 2014 World Health Organization (WHO) concept note on surveillance of HIVDR in adults initiating ART was undertaken from July 2017 to April 2018[10]. We first selected ART clinics using probability proportional to size sampling and then we recruited patients who met the eligibility criteria at each selected clinic as they register into HIV care. The survey included 14 ART clinics (one clinic was sampled twice) across eight provinces. The target estimated sample size was calculated at 345 (23 per clinic except the clinic that was sampled twice had 46) following the sampling method suggested in the 2014 WHO PDR concept note [10].

Patient selection

Eligibility criteria included being HIV positive, being aged ≥ 18 years, providing written informed consent, and either initiating ART with prior ART exposure (through prophylactic treatment including mothers on Option B+) or without prior ART exposure) or re-initiating ART (first or second line therapy) after a treatment interruption of ≥ 90 days.

Specimen collection, handling, and processing

Specimen collection, handling, and processing procedures followed the WHO HIVDR guidelines using dried blood spots (DBS) for HIVDR testing [11]. Consenting participants provided 500 μL of venous whole blood, which was spotted on Whatman 903 filter paper cards. DBS were dried at room temperature and sent by courier within three days of collection to central laboratories in Goroka and Port Moresby and stored at − 80 °C. DBS were shipped to a WHO-accredited laboratory at US CDC in Atlanta, GA, for HIVDR testing.

HIVDR genotyping

The protease and reverse transcriptase regions of the HIV-1 pol gene were genotyped [12]. Sequencing was performed using the Thermo Fisher (Waltham, MA, USA) HIV-1 Genotyping Kit Amplification and Cycle Sequencing Module Kit and analyzed on an ABI 3730 DNA Analyzer (Applied Biosystems; Waltham, MA, USA). The ReCALL software was used to edit the raw sequences and generate consensus sequences [13]. Sequence quality assurance was performed using genetic pairwise distances (2% cut-off ) and neighbour joining tree analyses, performed in MEGA to rule out possible sample contamination [14]. Sequences were classified as having low-level, intermediate, or high-level resistance according to the Stanford HIV database algorithm (version 8.5) and were aggregated as “HIV drug resistance”.

HIV PDR prevalence analysis

Data were analyzed using Stata version 14, StataCorp, Texas, USA. PDR prevalence rates were calculated at the national level and stratified by prior ART exposure status with respective confidence intervals. Some of the analyses were adjusted for survey weights and clustering.

Ethics

The study received ethics clearance from the Ethics Review Committee of the Western Pacific Regional Office of World Health Organization (2015.52. PNG.2.HSI), PNG Medical Research Advisory Committee (16.39) and PNG Institute of Medical Research Institutional Review Board (1605). This project was also reviewed in accordance with United States Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (US CDC) human research protection procedures. Informed consent was obtained from all the study participants.



## Results

Demographic and clinical characteristic of patients

The summary of participant recruitment and drug resistance analysis is depicted in Fig. 1. Of the 337 of participants enrolled; 268 (79.5%) were ART naïve and 69 (20.5%) had previous exposure to ART. All of those who had previous exposure to ART had interrupted treatment with none through PMTCT or pre-exposure prophylaxis. Most (207; 61.4%) of participants were female. The mean age was 31 years (range 18–67 years) (Table 1). Of the 236 (70%) participants with CD4 T-cell counts, the mean was 237 cells/mm3 (range 10–121 cells/mm3), and 61.9% had CD4-T-cell counts ≤ 250 cells/mm3 (Table 1). Of the 323 participants who had WHO Disease Staging assessed, 172 (53.3%) had stage III disease. Of the 312 participants who initiated first-line ART, 84% (n = 267) received a TDF-based regimen (Table 1). There were 25 participants that had no written records of first-line ART initiated either due to shortage of ART or they were treated for other infections and ART initiation was delayed at the time of survey.

Patient drug resistance profile

Of the total 337 DBS, 315 were successfully amplified with sequences available for analysis whilst 22 failed to amplify. PDR surveillance drug resistance mutations were detected in 51/315 of patients yielding an overall prevalence of any resistance mutations at 18.4% (95% CI 13.8–24.3%) (Table 2). NNRTI-related PDR mutations occurred in 17.8% (95% CI 13.6–23.0) of sequences whilst NRTI-related occurred in 5.6% (95% CI 1.6–17.1%). Eleven patients had SDRMs to both NNRTIs and NRTIs. There were no protease inhibitor-resistant mutations. The most frequent occurring NNRTI mutation was K103N/K103KN followed by Y181C, M184V was the most prevalent NRTI mutation. All sequences were subtype C except one was subtype A and another B. Of note, on CDC laboratory routine quality checks 59/315 samples showed > 98% genetic similarity, which indicates high homology.



## Discussion

Our study is the first nationally representative survey of PDR, and our findings have important implications for the national HIV response in PNG. The overall prevalence rate of the frequency of PDR mutations is high (18.4%) as is the PDR mutations to NNRTIs (17.8%); placing PNG among the top five countries with PDR rates exceeding > 10% [15]. As per the Global Action Plan on HIV Drug Resistance 2017–2021, countries reporting NNRTI-resistance prevalence of > 10% are recommended to change from an NNRTI to a non-NNRTI-based first-line ART regimen [16]. WHO now highly recommends dolutegravir (DTG), a potent integrase inhibitor with a high genetic barrier to HIVDR as the preferred first-line drug [17]. Additionally, DTG has minimal side effects, is affordable, and is increasingly available in many low- and middle-income countries: [18, 19] A DTG-containing regimen remains the most affordable treatment option for patients in PNG. Subsequent to the findings of this study, and the treatment advocacy that it resulted in, the Government of PNG procured new first line treatment and has, with its development partners, commenced ongoing transition to DTG.

With overall NNRTI-resistance prevalence rates of 17.8%, and 42.4% (Table 2) among the treatment-experienced, our findings suggest that NNRTI-containing regimens should be removed from use as first-line treatment in PNG. Changing the national treatment guidelines could halt HIVDR emergence. In addition to guideline changes and rolling out of DTG-based regimens, improvements in PNG’s health system, including improving availability of HIV drugs both at the national and facility level, efficient drug distribution systems to avoid stock outs, reducing attrition rates after 12 months on ART, and improving treatment adherence could help improve patient outcomes.

With the absence of routine HIVDR testing in PNG, HIV viral load monitoring could be useful in identifying early signs of adherence issues and/or treatment failure. Increased efforts are needed for an expansion of a quality HIV viral load testing program throughout the country, including providing such testing at point-of-care. In the absence of routine HIVDR testing if HIV viral load testing was widely available across the entire country (and people got their results in a timely manner) this could assist in understanding the emergence of further PDR. Our study showed that over half of the participants are presenting to clinics in the late stages (symptomatic) of the course of HIV infection and getting tested for HIV. This poses a challenge to the efforts to fast track the first 95 UNAIDS target where 95% of people who are living with HIV to know their HIV status. Although, HIV testing is available in the most parts# Conclusion

In conclusion, increased efforts, including the introduction of DTG as the preferred first-line drug and improving supply chain could improve treatment adherence, retention, and reduction of transmission of PDR. Moreover, expanding and incorporating DTG transition and viral load testing into routine HIV care is likely to result in reduced PDR rates and improve patient outcomes for people living with HIV in PNG.

# Resistance Analyses in Highly Treatment-Experienced People With Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) Treated With the Novel Capsid HIV Inhibitor Lenacapavir

1 Nicolas A. Margot,1 Vidula Naik,1 Laurie VanderVeen,1 Olena Anoshchenko,2 Renu Singh,2 Hadas Dvory-Sobol,3 Martin S. Rhee,3 and Christian Callebaut

Background. Lenacapavir (LEN) is a first-in-class inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) capsid function in clinical development for the treatment of heavily treatment-experienced (HTE) people with HIV (PWH) harboring multidrug resistance (MDR) in combination with an optimized background regimen (OBR). Here we describe resistance analyses conducted in the pivotal phase 2/3 CAPELLA study.

Methods. CAPELLA enrolled viremic HTE PWH with resistance to ≥3 of 4 of the main antiretroviral (ARV) classes and resistance to ≥2 ARV drugs per class. Baseline resistance analyses used commercial assays (HIV-1 protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase genotypic/phenotypic tests). Postbaseline resistance was evaluated in participants experiencing virologic failure.

Results. At baseline, 46% of participants had resistance to the 4 main ARV drug classes, with one-third of participants having exhausted all drugs from ≥3 of the 4 main ARV classes. Treatment with LEN + OBR for 26 weeks led to viral suppression in 81% of participants. Postbaseline resistance mutations to lenacapavir occurred in 8 participants (6 with M66I, 1 with K70H, 1 with Q67H + K70R) who were receiving unintended functional LEN monotherapy at the time of resistance selection.

Conclusions. LEN added to OBR led to high efficacy in this HTE patient population with MDR but could select for resistance when used unintentionally as functional monotherapy.

Keywords. HIV; capsid; lenacapavir; monotherapy; multidrug resistance; optimized background regimen.

Lenacapavir (LEN) is a first-in-class inhibitor of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) capsid

## METHODS

CAPELLA Study

Study GS-US-200-4625 (CAPELLA) is an ongoing phase 2/3 clinical study evaluating LEN in combination with an OBR in ARV treatment-experienced PWH with MDR. CAPELLA enrolled participants with MDR receiving a nonsuppressive treatment regimen and comprised 2 cohorts of participants: a randomized cohort (cohort 1, n = 36) that included a placebo-controlled 14-day LEN functional monotherapy period, and a nonrandomized cohort (cohort 2, n = 36) [11].

MDR was defined as resistance to ≥2 ARV medications from each of ≥3 of the 4 main classes of ARV drugs (NRTI, NNRTI, PI, INSTI) and plasma HIV-1 RNA ≥400 copies/mL at the screening visit while taking a failing regimen. In the presence of the reverse transcriptase mutation M184V/I, resistance to lamivudine and FTC did not count toward the total number of drugs with resistance for the NRTI drug class per protocol requirements.

Baseline Resistance Analyses

The preenrollment resistance profile of participants comprised data generated at the screening visit and/or historical data provided  by  the  clinical  investigators.  Resistance  testing  was conducted  at  screening  using  genotypic  and  phenotypic
assays  from  Monogram  Biosciences  (South  San  Francisco, California)  [13],  including  PhenoSense  GT,  GeneSeq Integrase,  PhenoSense  Integrase,  GenoSure  MG,  GenoSure Integrase, and/or Trofile/PhenoSense Entry. In addition, inves-tigators were allowed to provide historical resistance reports to support the resistance requirements for the study.HIV-1  CA  genotypic  and  phenotypic  data  at  study  entry were  determined  using  the  GenoSure  Gag-Pro  and PhenoSense  Gag-Pro  assays  (Monogram  Biosciences).  The GenoSure  Gag-Pro  assay  uses  next-generation  sequencing  to detect codon variants present at >10% frequency.

Baseline Overall Susceptibility Score Determination
For participants enrolled in the study on the basis of the resis-tance  assays  conducted  at  screening  (Monogram  assays),  the overall susceptibility score (OSS) for each ARV drug was pro-vided  electronically  by  Monogram  Biosciences.  For  partici-pants  enrolled  on  the  basis  of  historical  resistance  reports, resistance  mutations,  and  drug  scores  were  provided  directly by  investigators  through  an  electronic  data  capture  system. The OSS is the sum of the susceptibility scores from each indi-vidual drug component of the OBR. Fully active drugs contrib-uted a score of 1, while drugs with partial resistance had a score  of 0.5 and drugs with resistance had a score of 0

### Definition of Resistance Mutations
The list of major/primary resistance mutations for each of the
4  main  ARV  classes  was  derived  from  the  most  recent
International Antiviral Society–USA list [14] and other publi-cations [15] and included the following:

P225H, F227C, M230I/L

T66A/I/K, E92G/Q/V, G118R, F121C/Y, G140R, Y143C/H/R, S147G, Q148H/K/R, N155H/S, R263K.Known LEN resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) in CA included L56I, M66I, Q67H, K70N, N74D/S, and T107N [1].

Postbaseline Resistance Analyses
Resistance testing was performed for any participant meeting virologic failure (VF) criteria.

Suboptimal Virologic Response
Suboptimal  virologic  response  was  defined  as  HIV-1  RNA ≥50 copies/mL and <1 log10  HIV-1 RNA reduction from the start of oral LEN at the week 4 visit, confirmed at a scheduled or unscheduled visit at least 2 weeks following week 4.

### Virologic Rebound

Virologic rebound was defined as follows: at any visit, after achieving HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL, a rebound in HIV-1 RNA to ≥50 copies/mL that was subsequently confirmed at the following visit, or at any visit a >1 log10 increase in HIV-1 RNA from the nadir that was subsequently confirmed at the following visit.

### Viremic at Last Time Point

Any study participant with HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL at the study endpoint/discontinuation who did not meet any of the criteria above was also tested for resistance. Participants who were analyzed at week 26.

Resistance testing was conducted at Monogram Biosciences and consisted of genotypic and phenotypic analyses of CA, protease/reverse transcriptase, and integrase at the VF time points. In cases of assay failure at Monogram, genotyping of CA was tested at Seq-IT GmbH & Co. KG (Kaiserslautern, Germany).

### OBR Drug Plasma Concentration Quantitation

Plasma concentrations of darunavir (DRV), dolutegravir (DTG), FTC, and tenofovir (TFV) were determined using a validated liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry method with multiple reaction monitoring and electrospray ionization in the positive mode (QPS, LLC, Newark, Delaware). The bioanalytical method was validated over the calibrated ranges of 20–10 000 ng/mL for DRV, 20–20 000 ng/mL for DTG, 5–3000 ng/mL for FTC, and 0.3–300 ng/mL for TFV. All samples were analyzed in the timeframe supported by frozen stability storage data.

## RESULTS

Baseline Resistance Analyses

A total of 72 participants were enrolled in study 4625, distributed into 2 cohorts of 36. Resistance reports were obtained prior to enrollment to confirm that the resistance criteria for enrollment in the study were met. These reports were either generated from samples collected at screening (Monogram genotypic and phenotypic assays, n = 45/72) or from historical reports supplied by the investigators (various assays, n = 27/72).

For a subset of participants, both historical reports and screening reports were used to evaluate the baseline resistance% of Participants were viremic at week 26 in the absence of LEN resistance (n = 15). The OSS for each drug was obtained from the resistance reports.

The prevalence of major/primary RAMs at baseline for the 4 main ARV classes was high across drug classes, with 99% of participants harboring NRTI RAMs, 94% with NNRTI RAMs, 83% with PI RAMs, and 67% with INSTI RAMs.

The limited treatment options available for this HTE population were further emphasized by the median number of ARV agents with resistance, which approached the total number of ARV agents per class. Furthermore, close to 70% of participants had completely exhausted ARV options from ≥2 ARV classes, including one-third of participants who had no ARV options from ≥3 classes.

The NNRTI and INSTI classes were the most affected drug classes, having been exhausted in 64% and 56% of participants, respectively.

The high level of resistance in individual classes was associated with a high degree of overlap among ARV classes, showing that close to half of the participants had 4-class resistance while the remainder had 3-class resistance. The exception was a participant in the non-randomized cohort who had 3-class resistance in the presence of the NRTI mutation M184V. Mutation at M184 is quite common upon treatment failure, and its presence alone was not sufficient to fulfill the NRTI resistance criteria in the study.The presence of LEN resistance was also assessed at baseline. Of  the  62  participants  with  genotypic  and  phenotypic  data, none exhibited LEN RAMs, and all had phenotypic susceptibil-ity to LEN near wild-type level (average fold change compared to wild-type = 1.0, ranging from 0.3 to 1.7; Figure 3)


### Overall Susceptibility Scores of OBR

The composition of the OBR for each participant was selected by the study investigator and was based on the level of known resistance, tolerability, contraindication, availability, and prior experience with individual ARVs at the time of enrollment.

Details of individuals’ OBR and their treatment outcome at week 26 are provided (Supplementary Table 1). Of the 30 approved drugs for HIV treatment (4 INSTIs, 6 NNRTIs, 7 NRTIs, 9 PIs, and the 4 entry inhibitors enfuvirtide, fostemsavir [FTR], ibalizumab [IBA], and maraviroc), 17 drugs were used in the OBR in various combinations (Supplementary Table 1).

The drugs most often used in the OBR were tenofovir (79%, either as TAF [53%] or as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [26%]), FTC (68%), DRV (61%), DTG (50%), doravirine (26%), and IBA (24%) (Supplementary Table 1).

The level of resistance to drugs included in the OBR was reflected by the OSS of each individual OBR. Across the 72 participants, the median number of drugs in the OBR was 4, the median OSS of the OBR was 2, and the median number of fully active drugs in the OBR was 1 (Supplementary Table 2). These data indicate that the OBR was often composed of partially active drugs whose activity was affected by preexisting resistance, highlighting the inherent difficulties of identifying an effective treatment regimen.



### Participants With LEN-Associated CA RAMs

The virologic response experienced by the 8 participants with LEN-associated CA RAM emergence is shown in Supplementary Table 3. These participants experienced an average of 2.4 log10 HIV-1 RNA reduction (ranging from −3.6 to −1.0), achieved within an average of 5–6 weeks before experiencing viral rebound associated with LEN resistance. Four of these participants (participants 13, 26, 41, and 56; Supplementary Table 3) had no fully active ARVs in their OBR and were consequently in a situation of functional LEN monotherapy at the time of resistance development. Treatment options for these participants were limited based on the baseline resistance analysis, but 2 of them (participants 13 and 56) were able to resuppress HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL upon switching to active or partially active agents while maintaining LEN. Viral rebound to baseline level was observed in 2 of these 4 participants. The 4 other participants with LEN RAMs (participants 9, 36, 50, and 68; Supplementary Table 3) had an OBR that included at least 2 fully active agents. However, drug level measurements of key OBR drugs (DRV, DTG, FTC, TFV) (Supplementary Table 3) indicated that these drugs were not detected in the blood samples collected at the time of LEN resistance development.

## DISCUSSION

The CAPELLA study was designed to investigate the antiviral activity of LEN in people with limited treatment options due to extensive resistance to current ARVs. Baseline sequence analysis showed that nearly half of participants had resistance to the 4 main ARV classes, and constructing a treatment regimen for this population was further complicated by the extensive level of cross-resistance among agents within classes. As a result, exhaustion of at least 3 of the 4 main ARV classes was observed in one-third of participants, further emphasizing their limited treatment options and the potential benefit a new agent with a different mechanism of action could provide. Close to 70% of participants had at most 2 ARV classes from which fully active agents could be selected for their OBR, and for many participants, agents in the OBR were only partially active. Despite these restrictions in treatment options, 81% of participants who enrolled in the study were able to achieve durable viral suppression through 26 weeks of treatment with LEN + OBR. In this difficult-to-treat HTE population, suboptimal antiviral activity of the OBR may have limited the overall power of LEN in combination with other agents to drive viral suppression, as in comparison, LEN-containing regimens in treatment-naive participants were associated with 94% treatment responses through week 28. The treatment option limitations and the history of VF and development of resistance in this HTE population was also an important factor for the 8 participants with LEN resistance. Four of these participants had no fully active ARVs in their OBR. The 4 other participants had 2 or 3 fully active agents in their OBR, but plasma drug concentration measurements indicated poor adherence with the self-administered OBR. Thus, these 8 participants were essentially receiving functional monotherapy with LEN, and not surprisingly experienced virological rebound associated with LEN resistance. These cases illustrate the challenges faced by HTE patients and their providers in finding effective treatment regimens. Including fully or partially active medications in the OBR of these participants based on their resistance profile and encouraging and supporting adherence may make the difference between treatment failure due to unintended functional LEN monotherapy and durable virologic suppression.

Resistance to LEN in HTE Participants • JID 2022:226 (1 December) • 1989The LEN resistance mutations observed in the 8 participants 57% (cohort 1) and 42% (cohort 2) of participants having occurred at residues previously characterized during in vitro resistance selection studies, which mapped to the LEN binding site existing at the interface between 2 CA monomers within hexameric CA [1, 4, 16]. Although novel substitutions associated with LEN resistance were noted at residues such as Q67 and K70, most mutations observed in study participants were predicted based on in vitro experiments, confirming that LEN binding in vivo closely matches previous modeling conducted in vitro. This is consistent with LEN’s inhibitory activity in vivo being driven by binding to a defined site between CA monomers and not associated with interaction at cleavage sites within gag, as previously established [2]. Substitutions at position A105 (A105T or A105S) were observed in combination with other LEN-associated resistance mutations such as M66I and K70H, and may play a role in resistance to LEN, as another mutation at that position (A105E) was observed in resistance selection experiments using a close analog of LEN (GS-CA1) [17]. The potential role of these substitutions is currently under investigation.

Although LEN resistance was observed in 8 participants, 12 other participants who experienced VF did not have LEN resistance. These included 9 participants who eventually achieved HIV-1 RNA suppression <50 copies/mL, and 3 participants who remained viremic. This suggests that many difficult-to-treat PWH can eventually achieve virologic suppression while receiving LEN + OBR, and that active replication (observed up to week 78 after start of LEN in this study) while receiving LEN is not necessarily associated with development of LEN resistance. All but 1 of these 9 participants received at least 1 fully active drug within their OBR along with drugs with potential residual activity, and the combination of LEN + OBR was able to suppress viral replication while avoiding the emergence of resistance. Of note, 2 of the 3 participants who did not achieve suppression to <50 copies/mL still experienced an average HIV-1 RNA decline of 1.6 log10 copies/mL by week 26, indicating active viral inhibition from LEN + OBR. As indicated previously, inadequate adherence to agents from the OBR may have influenced the extent of the treatment response in these participants.

The challenge with treating HTE PWH with MDR was partially addressed with the recent approval of 2 new ARV drugs, FTR and IBA, although adherence to either drug may be difficult (FTR: twice daily oral dosing; IBA: every-2-weeks intravenous infusion). Recognizing limitations in comparisons across studies, the phase 3 studies of FTR and IBA [18, 19] and LEN (current study) were analogous as they were conducted in participants with similar treatment profiles, baseline resistance characteristics, and study duration, although these drugs were not compared directly in a single clinical study. Treatment efficacy varied across these studies, with 81% of participants having HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL at week 26 in the LEN study.
